correctness.rationale: The digit-split recurrence is algebraically exact. Nonnegative symmetric even-block coefficients satisfy a tridiagonal recurrence including the cyclic seam; an even/odd prefix interval induction covers all q=2h+1, including q=3 and both exceptional seam residues. Strict zero-residue positivity follows from the lower-length first half and subtraction of a nonpositive adjacent-residue prefix in the second half. The increasing base-b digit embedding preserves digit parity and residues when b≡−1 (mod q). Exact tests check 122,865 finite prefixes across q=3..31 and complete blocks up to length 119 for eight moduli; finite computations are not presented as the infinite proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Somu encompasses q divisible by b+1 asymptotically but its statements lack every-positive-cutoff signs. Drmota–Stoll gives all-prefix signs for q=3 under ordinary Thue–Morse but in other bases uses unrestricted digits; neither entails the universal sparse/alternating sign statement for every odd q.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Eventual positive bias does not imply positivity at initial cutoffs. The existing all-prefix q=3 result is one modulus, whereas the new induction covers every odd q and signs at nonzero residues. The classical unrestricted sampling and sparse sampling match only at b=2; no deduction from the stronger-looking unrestricted general-base asymptotics is evident.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Binary-alternating residue counts are identical, via b≡−1 mod q and order-preserving digit embedding, to sparse base-b q-residue counts. Checked both formulations; the source that studies the sparse embedding asserts eventual, not uniform prefix, positivity.

originality.rationale: Somu 2015, Theorem 1.1, treats the same restricted 0/1 base-b integer set and proves only sufficiently-large cutoff positivity; this proof gives all positive cutoffs and every residue for all odd divisors of b+1. Drmota–Stoll 2008 treats ordinary arithmetic progressions of full base-g integers, not the sparse 0/1 restriction except g=2, and its special q=3 finite-prefix result does not imply the arbitrary odd-modulus alternating-digit sign law. Distinct statements and absence of a dominating theorem in the inspected materials support best-knowledge novelty, with residual priority risk.
residual_risks: The full text of Drmota–Skałba 2000 was not inspected; its stated scope is ordinary residue sums, not the sparse-base all-modulus theorem.
Unindexed or differently formulated priority results, especially finite automata descriptions of signed alternating-digit sums, could imply the theorem.
The result is verified by an ordinary self-review; it has not undergone independent peer review.

value.rationale: The pre-existing explicit sparse-base Newman problem provided only eventually-positive residue zero results, leaving initial cutoffs and all other residues unresolved. A universal sign pattern indexed by residue distance, and an every-cutoff strengthening for all even bases and odd q|b+1, is a structural classification applying to infinitely many naturally ordered digit sets and directly sharpens the motivating theorem.
